title: A hymn in Suhi
hook: Suhi holds the Lavan, and Guru Nanak's paired poems of the unskilled and the skilled bride

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Suhi, which opens with a clean vessel, milk and a churn, and your line was union. Did you clear the vessel before something that mattered? Day one thousand ninety-five.

Skills. Job applications ask for them, dating profiles hint at them, and family weddings have their own unwritten list: can she cook, can he earn, will they fit in. In the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak sets two poems side by side. One is called Kuchaji, the unskilled bride. The next is Suchaji, the skilled bride. And the skill that wins the second poem its name is on nobody's list. Today: a hymn in Suhi.
screen: `CAN SHE COOK, CAN HE EARN.` → `TWO POEMS SIDE BY SIDE.` → `A SKILL ON NOBODY'S LIST.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Suhi holds the Lavan, the four rounds that marry a Sikh couple; we walked them earlier on this path. Near them sit poems where the bride is the soul and the husband is the Lord. Second, the unskilled bride. In paraphrase, she says: I'm unskilled, with faults beyond counting; how can I go to my Husband? The other brides seem each one better than the next; who would even know my name? The friends who have enjoyed their Lord sit in the shade of the mango trees. I have none of their virtues. It's a list of failures, and she says it out loud, without dressing it up. Third, the skilled bride, and here's the surprise. She doesn't list talents. In paraphrase: when you are with me, I have everyone; you, my Master, are all my wealth. With you within, I live in peace. Then the line that turns the poem: by your will come thrones and greatness, and by your will a beggar's wandering. She isn't skilled because life went well. She's skilled because she can say the same thing on a throne and with a begging bowl: whatever comes, you are my wealth. Fourth, put the two together. The poems don't hand out prizes for beauty, wit or cooking. The unskilled bride's honesty about her faults is where the path begins. The skilled bride's skill is acceptance of the Lord's will, which Sikhs call bhana. That's today's line: the skilled bride.
screen: `SUHI HOLDS THE LAVAN.` · `KUCHAJI: I'M UNSKILLED, FULL OF FAULTS.` · `SUCHAJI: YOU ARE MY WEALTH.` · `THRONE OR BEGGING BOWL, BY YOUR WILL.` · then, large: `THE SKILLED BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Suhi shabad, or try both brides' words. If you can, play a recording of Suchaji or of the Lavan. Otherwise, sit and breathe. For the first minute, be the unskilled bride for a moment: let one fault come to mind, plainly, without a speech of excuses. Just name it. For the second minute, set beside it one thing in your life that's going well, and one that isn't, and hold them both in open hands, the throne and the bowl. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once over both. If you don't, let them rest side by side. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Suhi. Guru Nanak's paired poems: Kuchaji, the bride who names her faults, and Suchaji, whose skill is to say you are my wealth on a throne or with a bowl. Today's word.
Your line: the skilled bride. Today, when something goes well and when something goes badly, try saying the same short sentence about both, and notice what it does. Day one thousand ninety-five.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Kuchaji and Suchaji are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and some Sikh teachers use them to explain bhana, acceptance of God's will; the Lavan in the same raga are sung at the Anand Karaj.

fork.setup: you're the bride in Suchaji. one season brings a throne; the next, a begging bowl. what do you say?
options: thank God for the throne and complain about the bowl.
both come by your will; you are my wealth.
fork.reveal: by your will thrones and greatness, by your will a beggar's wandering. her skill is that you are my wealth holds in both.

original.note: suchaji, the skilled bride; kuchaji is her unskilled sister poem.

trapdoor: what you thought: a skilled bride is a good homemaker.
what it means: in Guru Nanak's Suhi poems the bride is the soul, and her skill is acceptance: you are my wealth, on a throne or with a bowl.
what a scholar hears: Kuchaji and Suchaji (around ang 762) form a pair, a confession of faults beside a hymn of bhana, the acceptance of the Lord's will, placed in Suhi near the Lavan.

sources.ref: Suhi Mahalla 1, Kuchaji, Ang 762 (I'm unskilled and full of faults; each bride seems better than the next; friends in the mango shade)
